title: Response to “Exponential challenges in unbiasing quantum Monte Carlo algorithms with quantum computers”
abstract_summary: This is a response to a preprint by Mazzola and Carleo analyzing exponential challenges for the QC-QMC algorithm. The authors argue that such exponential measurement overheads depend critically on the choice of QMC method, the physical system, and the forms of trial and walker wavefunctions, and provide additional numerics (including 1D TFIM examples) to show regimes where QC-QMC remains viable. They conclude that QC-QMC may still offer practical advantages for certain problems and call for further research to identify favorable system/method combinations.
methodology_description: This work is a computational/numerical response study analyzing exponential-scaling challenges in the QC-QMC framework. The authors compare different QMC flavors (QC-AFQMC vs QC-GFMC) and analyze system dependence using the one-dimensional transverse field Ising model (TFIM) with periodic boundary conditions, H = -J sum σz_k σz_{k+1} - Γ sum σx_k, for varying Γ/J and system sizes L. They evaluate the dependence on trial and walker wavefunction choices by (i) using analytical trial forms (e.g., |ΨT> = exp[λ sum σx_i](|↑↑…> + |↓↓…>) with λ=0.127), (ii) sampling computational-basis states from |ΨT|^2, and (iii) constructing walkers as simple product states or as more sophisticated non-orthogonal states generated by 1..L spin flips from a complex trial |ΨMC>. Numerical observables are the overlap distribution of basis states with |ΨT>, local energy per site, and GFMC total energy error as a function of the number of measurements M (analyzed versus M^{-1/2}) and system size. Multiple independent simulation runs are performed for statistics (16 independent runs per overlap/local-energy data point; GFMC averages over 128 runs). They also discuss mapping TFIM to fermions for AFQMC and contrast regimes (Γ/J=1.0 vs Γ/J=0.5) to illustrate method/system/trial dependence of exponential measurement overhead.
experimental_setup: Classical numerical simulations run on Columbia University's Shared Research Computing Facility; GFMC sampling of computational-basis states from |ΨT|^2, analysis performed for TFIM systems with L up to 12, and multiple independent runs (16 for overlap/local-energy, 128 for GFMC averages).
experiment_process: 1) Choose QMC flavor (GFMC used for the presented TFIM numerics; AFQMC discussed conceptually). 2) Select Hamiltonian parameters and system size (TFIM with specified Γ/J, L). 3) Define trial wavefunction(s): e.g., |ΨT> = exp[λ Σ σx_i](|↑…>+|↓…>) with λ=0.127, and |ΨMC> used in comparisons. 4) Prepare walker ensembles: (a) single computational-basis-state walkers (product states) and (b) sophisticated non-orthogonal walkers generated by spin flips from |ΨMC>. 5) Sample computational-basis states from the probability distribution |ΨT|^2 with varying numbers of measurements M. 6) For each sampled walker, estimate overlap magnitude (and sign where applicable) and compute local energy per site. 7) Repeat sampling for multiple independent runs (16) to estimate variance; average GFMC results over 128 independent runs. 8) Analyze overlap distributions, local-energy variances, and GFMC energy error scaling vs M and system size; compare regimes Γ/J=1.0 and 0.5.
experiment_output: Outputs are numerical diagnostic metrics: distributions of overlaps between trial and basis/walker states, local energy per site (with variance), and GFMC total energy error per site plotted as a function of number of measurements M (and displayed vs M^{-1/2}) and system size L. Comparisons/plots contrast different Γ/J regimes and walker complexity; no financial or classical ML evaluation metrics are used.

key_findings: [supported] The exponential measurement challenge in QC-QMC depends on the choice of QMC method (e.g., QC-AFQMC vs QC-GFMC).
[supported] For the 1D TFIM mapped to a non-interacting fermionic Hamiltonian, AFQMC (and QC-AFQMC) is exact (no QMC sampling required).
[supported] The severity of exponential challenges in QC-GFMC depends on the system parameters (e.g., Γ/J); numerics show markedly different behavior for Γ/J = 1.0 versus Γ/J = 0.5.

[supported] A specific variational trial state (|ΨT⟩ = exp[λ Σ σx_i](|↑↑...⟩ + |↓↓...⟩) with λ=0.127) reproduces the exact ground-state energy better than 99.8% for L = 6–12 in the Γ/J = 0.5 TFIM example.

[supported] Using more sophisticated (non-product) walker wavefunctions that are closer to the trial state sharpens the overlap distribution and greatly reduces local energy variance in QC-GFMC numerics.
[supported] The use of sophisticated walkers can introduce a sign problem even in models that are otherwise sign-problem free.

[supported] For some finite-size problems studied by the authors, exponential measurement-scaling was not the practical bottleneck; the authors demonstrated noise-resilient quantum simulations up to 16 qubits in prior work.

[speculative] There is no proof that the exponential overlap/measurement challenge is always the computational bottleneck for QC-QMC across all systems and settings; the authors argue it may be avoidable/deferred in some regimes.

[speculative] QC-QMC can be more efficient in quantum resources and measurement overhead than VQE and QPE when adding more basis functions while keeping particle number fixed, because it obtains electron correlation outside the qubit space.
[speculative] Identifying specific combinations of method, system, and trial/walker choices could enable practical quantum advantage for QC-QMC; this remains an open research direction.
results_summary: The authors respond to a critique by demonstrating that exponential difficulties in estimating overlaps for QC-QMC are not universal but depend strongly on the chosen classical QMC flavor, the physical system, and the forms of trial and walker wavefunctions. They present numerical comparisons for the 1D TFIM at Γ/J = 1.0 and Γ/J = 0.5, showing much more favorable behavior (sharper overlap distribution and weaker system-size dependence of GFMC energy vs measurement count) in the Γ/J = 0.5 regime when using a high-quality trial state. They also show that using sophisticated, non-product walkers can concentrate weight and reduce local-energy variance, though at the possible cost of inducing a sign problem. The authors emphasize that for some mapped non-interacting cases QC-AFQMC is exact, that they have demonstrated noise-resilient quantum simulations up to 16 qubits in prior work, and that QC-QMC may be comparatively efficient versus other quantum algorithms in certain regimes. They frame practical quantum advantage for QC-QMC as an open, system- and method-dependent research question.
performance_claims: [supported] The trial wavefunction |ΨT⟩ = exp[λ Σ σx_i](|↑...⟩ + |↓...⟩) with λ = 0.127 reproduces the exact ground-state energy better than 99.8% for L = 6–12 in the Γ/J = 0.5 TFIM.
[supported] The authors previously performed accurate quantum simulations up to 16 qubits, which they cite as evidence of noise resilience (from their original Nature work).
quantum_advantage_detail: The authors do not claim a demonstrated, general quantum advantage; rather they argue that QC-QMC may enable practical advantage for specific combinations of QMC method, system, and trial/walker choices, supported by targeted numerics but not by a general proof or broad experimental demonstration.
limitations: Quantum computers can only efficiently approximate wavefunction amplitudes up to an additive error ε, and when overlaps ⟨ΨT|φ⟩ decay exponentially with system size the number of measurements needed to maintain signal-to-noise will grow exponentially.
Exponential challenges are method-dependent: numerical examples showing difficulties for QC-GFMC do not necessarily apply to other QC-QMC variants (e.g., QC-AFQMC).

System dependence: certain Hamiltonian parameter regimes (example: 1D TFIM at Γ/J = 1) produce overlap distributions that make QC-GFMC measurement overheads large, while other regimes (e.g., Γ/J = 0.5 or Γ/J = 0) are more benign.

Walker and trial wavefunction dependence: performance of QC-QMC critically depends on the choice/construction of trial and walker wavefunctions; poor choices yield unfavorable overlap distributions and large local energy variance.
Use of sophisticated walkers complicates implementation and can introduce a sign problem even in models that would otherwise be sign-problem-free.
No zero-variance principle: even with good trials, there is not a guarantee of eliminating sampling variance entirely.

Fundamental complexity limits: because ground-state problems are QMA-hard, all known quantum ground-state algorithms (including QC-QMC) will be efficient for some systems and inefficient for others; direct cost comparisons require running algorithms on target hardware.
[inferred] Measurement overhead may become the computational bottleneck for practical, larger finite-size problems or for systems where amplitudes are extremely small across many basis states.
[inferred] Preparing more sophisticated walkers and trials may require additional classical/quantum resources or algorithmic complexity that offsets measurement benefits.
[inferred] Trade-offs (e.g., improved overlaps versus inducing a sign problem) may limit applicability across problem classes.
[inferred] There is no general evidence that QC-QMC will provide practical advantage across a broad class of problems; its efficacy is likely case-specific.
[inferred] Choosing the optimal QMC flavor and configuring trial/walker ansätze for a given system is nontrivial and may be a significant practical obstacle.

key_ideas: #idea:quantum-advantage — QC-QMC (quantum-computer-assisted QMC) may still offer practical advantages in specific problems/regimes; exponential measurement overhead is not a universal show-stopper.

#idea:hybrid-approach — The severity of measurement overhead in QC-QMC depends critically on the QMC flavor (e.g., AFQMC vs GFMC), the choice of trial and walker wavefunctions, and system specifics; careful hybrid design can reduce sampling cost.

#idea:near-term-feasibility — Numerical simulations on finite TFIM instances (L up to 12) show regimes where variational trial states achieve >99.8% ground-state energies and where measurement-scaling is not the dominant bottleneck; authors cite prior noise-resilient simulations up to ~16 qubits.

#idea:hybrid-approach — Using more sophisticated non-product walkers (closer to the trial state) sharpens overlap distributions and reduces local-energy variance, improving GFMC performance though possibly reintroducing a sign problem.
#idea:quantum-advantage — AFQMC can be exact (no QMC sampling) for systems mappable to non-interacting fermions (e.g., 1D TFIM mapping), illustrating system-dependent opportunities for QC-AFQMC.
contradictions: The authors directly counter the blanket claim in 2022_Mazzola_ExponentialChallenges that exponential measurement overhead universally prevents QC-QMC, showing via TFIM numerics that overheads depend on QMC variant, system parameters, and trial/walker choice.

They demonstrate that for TFIM mapped to non-interacting fermions AFQMC/ QC-AFQMC is effectively exact (no sampling bottleneck), contradicting general statements that QC-QMC always suffers exponential scaling.

They note that while sophisticated walkers reduce variance and measurement cost, they can reintroduce a sign problem — contradicting any simplistic claim that increased walker complexity uniformly improves scalability.
